Q: How to access the GMail API to perform mass deletions of a large GMail Account A:

Several steps needed to be added here to get my code to work.

The original error:

google.auth.exceptions.RefreshError: ('invalid_scope: Bad Request', {'error': 'invalid_scope', 'error_description': 'Bad Request'})

This brought me to a second problem:

Hopefully, this tale will help someone in this situation.

Q: How do I solve this type hint error "Unexpected type(s)" in PyCharm? A:

The variable redefinition seems to be the main problem. I recommend avoiding the re-assignment in this case, since working around it seems more troublesome than worth it.

From what I've gathered in the comments, the current filename variable (used in the if clause, and on the right side of the assignment to the new variable), is atually more akin to something like filename_suffix (or suffix for short).

Inlining the exerpt you mentioned in your comments, and presuming the type of datum_content_type to be str, we get:

import datetime

from typing import reveal_type

suffix: str | None = None
datum_content_type: str = ''

if suffix: #  i.e. not None
    fn = str(datetime.datetime.now()).replace(":", "-").replace(".", "-") + " - " + datum_content_type + " - " + suffix
    reveal_type(fn) # `str` in inlay hint, corroborated by MyPy.
    with open("files\\" + fn, "wb") as f:
        pass

With no more warnings in the with line :)

Two (tangential) notes:

  1. Please be aware that checking if s: ..., when s is str | None, does not execute the code block if the s is an empty string. This behavior may be desired or not, but be mindful of it. This may trip you up if you come from a C background.

  2. I strongly recommend explicitly choosing how your timestamps are formatted with strftime, instead of relying on the default behavior of datetime.__str__, which is to invoke datetime.isoformat. Luckily (?), in Python, the datetime objects returned by datetime.now are always timezone-naïve, which means consistent string formatting. However, in other languages or scenarios, not explicitly specifying whether to include the timezone in the formatted string can cause a world of hurt later on. This would also have the added benefit of removing the need for the str.replace calls, since you can just set the desired separator(s) in the format template directly :D

Q: How to handle the ... parameter when programming with dplyr A:

As noted in Konrad's answer, you can use rlang::enquos() to capture the ... arguments as a list of quosures, which you can then iterate over like any regular list. Each element can be injected back into dplyr verbs with !! and converted to a string name with rlang::as_label():

library(dplyr)

myfunc <- function(data, ...) {
  vars <- rlang::enquos(...)
  
  for (var in vars) {
    nm <- rlang::as_label(var)
    data <- data |>
      group_by(!!var) |>
      mutate(!!paste0(nm, "_mean") := mean(!!var))
  }
  data
}

iris |> myfunc(Sepal.Width, Sepal.Length)

#> # A tibble: 150 × 7
#> # Groups:   Sepal.Length [35]
#>    Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width Species Sepal.Width_mean
#>           <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <fct>              <dbl>
#>  1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2 setosa               3.5
#>  2          4.9         3            1.4         0.2 setosa               3  
#>  3          4.7         3.2          1.3         0.2 setosa               3.2
#>  4          4.6         3.1          1.5         0.2 setosa               3.1
#>  5          5           3.6          1.4         0.2 setosa               3.6
#>  6          5.4         3.9          1.7         0.4 setosa               3.9
#>  7          4.6         3.4          1.4         0.3 setosa               3.4
#>  8          5           3.4          1.5         0.2 setosa               3.4
#>  9          4.4         2.9          1.4         0.2 setosa               2.9
#> 10          4.9         3.1          1.5         0.1 setosa               3.1
#> # ℹ 140 more rows
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: Sepal.Length_mean <dbl>

Created on 2026-07-07 with reprex v2.1.1

Here, rlang::enquos(...) captures all ... arguments as unevaluated quosures, then iterating over the list gives you one quosure per variable. !!var injects the quosure back into dplyr verbs (group_by, mutate, etc.). rlang::as_label(var) extracts the variable name as a string for naming new columns. And finally := is needed on the left-hand side of mutate when the column name is computed programmatically.

This is equivalent to your working cols version but allows bare unquoted variable names in the function call.

Q: GitHub Actions Status Check Pending A:

Try manually setting status with this Github Actions snippet:

# We must set the commit status manually
      # Reference: https://github.com/bahmutov/eleventy-example/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci.yml#L27
      - name: Staging Tests ✅
        if: ${{ success() }}
        # set the merge commit status check
        # using GitHub REST API
        # see https://docs.github.com/en/rest/reference/repos#create-a-commit-status
        run: |
          curl --request POST \
          --url https://api.github.com/repos/${{ github.repository }}/statuses/${{ github.sha }} \
          --header 'authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}' \
          --header 'content-type: application/json' \
          --data '{
            "context": "Staging Tests",
            "state": "success",
            "description": "Staging tests passed",
            "target_url": "https://github.com/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}"
          }'
      - name: Staging Tests 🚨
        if: ${{ failure() }}
        # set the merge commit status check
        # using GitHub REST API
        # see https://docs.github.com/en/rest/reference/repos#create-a-commit-status
        run: |
          curl --request POST \
          --url https://api.github.com/repos/${{ github.repository }}/statuses/${{ github.sha }} \
          --header 'authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}' \
          --header 'content-type: application/json' \
          --data '{
            "context": "Staging Tests",
            "state": "failure",
            "description": "Staging tests failed",
            "target_url": "https://github.com/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}"
          }'

Q: How can I run a.out file in visual studio code automatically? A:

You can compile and run with various ways. Here's 3:

1. Add a task to run your executable.

Something like:

{
    "version": "2.0.0",
    "tasks": [
        {
            "label": "build hello world",
            "type": "shell",
            "command": "g++",
            "args": [
                "-g", "helloworld.cpp"
            ],
            "group": {
                "kind": "build",
                "isDefault": true
            }
        },
        {
            "label": "build and run hello world",
            "type": "shell",
            "command": "${workspaceFolder}/a.out",
            "dependsOn": "build hello world"
        }
    ]
}

2. Using a Visual Studio Code extension:

Such as:

C/C++ Compile Run

After installing, there are several Command Palette options for "CompileRun" to compile/run with default/custom options, or you can use the F6/F7 shortcut.

Several other similar extensions do the same. Search for "c/c++ run" in the Extensions Marketplace.

3. Old fashioned way:

Simply open a new terminal in VS Code and run the executable the old-fashioned way ;-)

./a.out
